meaning:
The idiom "get the ball rolling" means to start an activity, project, or process, often to build momentum or encourage others to join in.

Usage Examples

• Work & Projects: "Let's get the ball rolling on the new campaign by scheduling a kickoff meeting."
• Meetings & Discussions: "At the meeting, she tried to get the ball rolling by asking a few questions."
• Social Settings: "Nobody was on the dance floor, so I decided to get the ball rolling."

Synonyms & Variants

• Synonyms: kick things off, get things started, set in motion, initiate, break the ice.
• Common Variants: "Set the ball rolling" or "start the ball rolling" mean the same thing. "Keep the ball rolling" means to maintain momentum or continue an activity.

To start from scratch means to begin something completely from the beginning, without using prior work, pre-made materials, or existing progress. According to Merriam-Webster, it refers to starting from a point where nothing has been done yet, while the Cambridge Dictionary defines it as starting completely from the beginning.

Usage Examples

• Projects & work: "The first design failed, so the team had to start from scratch."
• Cooking & baking: "She baked the cake from scratch instead of using a boxed mix."
• Learning & business: "He built the company from scratch with no outside funding."

Synonyms & Opposites

• Synonyms: start from zero, begin anew, start fresh, build from the ground up
• Opposites: continue where you left off, build on existing work

"Spread the word" is a phrase or idiom that means to tell many people about something or share information widely.

Usage Examples

• "Spread the word that the meeting starts at 10 AM."
• "She posted on social media to spread the word about her new shop."
• "People are spreading the word about the community clean-up event."

Synonyms

• Tell others
• Let people know
• Pass on the message
• Inform or notify
• Circulate or share

"Paid off" (past tense/participle of pay off) means to finish paying a debt in full or to succeed and bring good results after effort.

Main Meanings & Usage Examples

• Pay a debt completely: Finish paying off money owed on a loan, bill, or mortgage.
	• Example: "She finally paid off her student loan."
• Bring success or profit: Produce positive results, rewards, or financial gains after time or hard work.
	• Example: "All those extra hours of practice paid off at the tournament."
• Pay wages upon leaving a job: Give an employee all owed wages when they leave or are dismissed.
	• Example: "The company paid off the staff when the branch closed."
• Bribe or hush money (informal): Pay someone secretly to stay quiet, avoid trouble, or act dishonestly.
	• Example: "He tried to pay off the witness."

A shoestring budget is a financial plan or project that operates with a very small, tight, or barely sufficient amount of money.

Key Characteristics

• Scarcity of Funds: There is little to no extra money for non-essential expenses.
• High Resourcefulness: It relies heavily on DIY methods, creative problem-solving, bartering, or low-cost alternatives rather than hiring outside help or buying brand-new items.
• Common Contexts: Often used when describing indie films, startup businesses, political campaigns, or households living with strict financial limits.

Origin of the Phrase

The idiom originated in the United States in the late 19th century. While the exact allusion is debated, popular theories suggest it refers to the slender, thin shape of a shoestring symbolizing a bare-minimum resource, or to early peddlers and immigrants who started trading with very cheap goods like shoelaces

meaning:
"Got home" is the past tense of "get home," meaning to arrive back at your house, apartment, or place of residence after being out or away.

Usage Examples

• "I got home around seven last night."
• "She just got home from work and is making tea."
• "Once I got home, I took off my shoes and rested."

"Whip up" is a phrasal verb that primarily means to make or prepare something quickly (often food), or to stir up strong emotions or excitement.

Core Meanings

• Make or prepare quickly (informal): Put together a meal, snack, or simple project fast and easily.
• Stir up emotions or excitement: Cause people to feel strong emotions, interest, or enthusiasm—or cause wind to lift dust, water, or smoke.
• Beat rapidly (literal): Whisk ingredients like cream or egg whites until light and frothy.

Usage Examples

• "Give me ten minutes and I'll whip up some scrambled eggs."
• "She whipped up a quick slide deck before the meeting."
• "The speech whipped up enthusiasm among the supporters."
• "Gusty winds whipped up dust across the field."

"Out of the blue" means completely unexpected, sudden, or without prior warning. It can describe good news, bad news, or any surprising event.

Usage Examples

• "She called me out of the blue after years of not speaking."
• "Out of the blue, he announced that he was resigning."
• "We were having dinner when, out of the blue, she mentioned moving abroad."

Synonyms

• Unexpectedly
• Suddenly
• Out of nowhere
• All of a sudden
• Without warning

Out of is a preposition used to express movement away from the inside, lack or depletion, origin or cause, and selection from a group.
According to the Cambridge Dictionary and Merriam-Webster, its main meanings include:

Core Meanings & Usage Examples

• Movement or location: Moving from inside to outside, or being beyond a limit.
	• Example: She walked out of the room or moved out of sight.
• Lack or depletion: Having no more of something left.
	• Example: We are out of milk, or I ran out of time.
• Origin, material, or cause: Where something comes from, what it is made of, or the reason behind an action.
	• Example: A house built out of wood, or acting out of fear.
• Selection or proportion: Choosing a part from a larger group or total.
	• Example: Three out of five students passed. (On English Language Learners Stack Exchange, opinions on using "out of" with improper fractions differ, though users generally note it represents a part of a total or ratio).

Halfway through (also written half way through) means at the middle point of a period of time, an event, a task, or a sequence. It shows that you have completed about half of something and have half left.

Usage Examples

• Time or events: "We left halfway through the movie."
• Tasks or projects: "They are halfway through building the house."
• Reading or studying: "I realized the plot twist halfway through the book."
As noted in the Cambridge Dictionary, it is commonly followed by a noun or an -ing verb (e.g., halfway through dinner or halfway through filming). Merriam-Webster also shows it used on its own at the end of a clause, such as "The teacher stopped the movie halfway through".

Synonyms and Related Phrases

Depending on the context, you can use similar expressions:
• Midway through or in the middle of (general time, events, or tasks)
• At the halfway mark or at the midpoint (often used for races, projects, or milestones)
• Midstream (often used for processes or projects already in progress)

meaning:
"Keep an eye" (usually "keep an eye on" or "keep an eye out") means to watch, monitor, or look after someone or something carefully.

Common Meanings

• Keep an eye on someone/something: Watch over someone or something to keep them safe, check their progress, or prevent trouble. According to Cambridge Dictionary, it also means staying informed about someone's behavior.
• Keep an eye out (for something): Stay alert and look carefully for a specific person, object, or event.

Usage Examples

• "Can you keep an eye on my bag while I grab a coffee?"
• "We need to keep an eye on our monthly expenses."
• "Keep an eye out for any sales during the weekend."

Synonyms

• Watch, monitor, observe, look after, supervise, stay alert.
